places.title: Green Bay, Wisconsin
places.summary: Born October 4, 1931, to William and Marie Stegmeier. His colleague’s memorial preserves the birthplace and date.

photo.title: Downtown Green Bay in 1930
photo.caption: Downtown Green Bay in 1930, the year before Bill was born there.

places.title: Elgin, North Dakota
places.summary: The census finds eight-year-old Bill living with his parents and two younger sisters in Elgin. It also reports rural Grant County residence in 1935.

photo.alt: A 1936 Grant County farm framed by trees killed by drought and grasshoppers.
photo.title: Rural Grant County during the Dust Bowl
photo.caption: Rural Grant County in July 1936—the county where Bill spent part of his childhood. This is a regional view, rather than an identified Stegmeier home.

places.title: Minneapolis, Minnesota
places.summary: The veterans register records his entry into the United States Marine Corps here on December 18, 1951.

photo.caption: Minneapolis on November 8, 1951, about six weeks before Bill entered the Marines there.

places.title: Yuma, Arizona
places.summary: Bill and Jean Cromer married in Yuma on January 2, 1953, during his Marine Corps years.

places.title: Camp Pendleton, California
places.summary: Records place him in a signal company at Camp Pendleton and later in a training regiment. He separated here as a corporal on December 3, 1953. A posting in Korea remains unestablished.

places.title: Fort Collins, Colorado
places.summary: Bill earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees at Colorado State University. Their dates have not yet been established.

places.title: Brookings, South Dakota
places.summary: A USDA report issued in February 1969 records that he had resumed graduate study at South Dakota State. It gives no exact enrollment or completion date.

places.title: Garden City, Kansas
places.summary: His Kansas State career began at Garden City in 1958. He studied familiar grains and possible alternative crops before moving to Hays.

photo.alt: Black-and-white aerial photograph of the Garden City Branch Experiment Station and its surrounding fields, reproduced in a 1957 station history.
photo.title: The Garden City station before Bill’s arrival
photo.caption: The Garden City station in its 1957 anniversary history, published one year before Bill arrived. The photograph’s exact date is unrecorded.

places.title: Hays, Kansas
places.summary: At Hays, Bill bred pearl millet and sunflower and explored other crops. He worked at the station from 1971 until his retirement in May 1998.

photo.alt: Color aerial photograph of the Hays experiment station from a brochure published in September 1984.
photo.title: The Hays station from the air
photo.caption: The Hays station in a September 1984 brochure, during Bill’s years there. The photograph’s exact date is unrecorded.
photo.credit: Kansas State University · © Kansas State University

crops.name: Pearl millet
crops.work: At Hays, Bill selected for earlier flowering, shorter plants and larger seed. His stocks, further selected at ICRISAT in India, became 842A/B and 843A/B: parents for commercial hybrids and future breeding.

parts.name: Grain head
parts.text: A dense, elongated head holds many small grains. Fine bristles give the head its bottle-brush outline.

parts.name: Leaf blades
parts.text: Long, narrow grass blades arch from the stem. The illustrations show each crop at its own scale.

parts.name: Jointed stem
parts.text: Leaves attach around the stem at sheathing bases. The joints are called nodes.

metrics.label: acres in India in a given year, reported by 1997
promising ICRISAT seed parents with 843B in their pedigrees, 1981–1998

crops.impact: Earlier maturity could fit a harvest into a short rainy season. HHB 67, with 843A as its seed parent, matured in about 65–70 days. Sharing these parents let other breeders combine that trait with local adaptation and disease resistance.
crops.context: The acreage estimate covers hybrids descended from the Hays program. The 49 lines are one ICRISAT breeding group, rather than all Indian hybrids. These were achievements of an international collaboration.

crops.name: Sunflower
crops.work: Bill bred sunflower at Hays for yield and resistance to insects and disease. He also cooperated in Kansas performance trials that compared commercial hybrids under local conditions.

parts.name: Flower head
parts.text: What looks like one large flower is a head of many small flowers: yellow ray florets around a central disk of florets.

parts.name: Toothed leaves
parts.text: The broad leaves have toothed edges and distinct leaf stalks. Leaf shape changes with position on the plant.

parts.name: Stem
parts.text: The upright stem supports the leaves and heavy head. Cultivated sunflower forms vary in branching and head size.

metrics.label: lb of seed per acre across hybrids at Hays, 1994
seed oil content in the same Hays trial

crops.impact: An oilseed crop offered farmers another product to sell. Comparing seed yield, oil yield, maturity and lodging helped them judge which hybrids might suit their farms. The station history credits his breeding work with helping sunflower gain acceptance in Kansas.
crops.context: These are trial results for commercial and experimental entries, rather than gains caused by Bill’s breeding. Late-season drought stressed the 1994 crop; the report recommends comparing several years and locations.

crops.name: Canola
crops.work: Bill was a Hays cooperator in the Great Plains canola research network. Trials tested winter survival, flowering and yield to identify oilseed material suited to the region.

parts.name: Four-petaled flowers
parts.text: Each flower has four yellow petals in a cross. Buds occur above open flowers as the flowering shoot grows.

parts.name: Slender seed pods
parts.text: Long, narrow pods develop below the flowers. Botanists call these pods siliques.

parts.name: Lower leaves
parts.text: Lower leaves are lobed and blue-green. Upper leaves are smaller and clasp the stem.

metrics.label: planted in 12 states for the 1997 advanced nursery
sites produced harvest data in that season

crops.impact: Canola offered edible oil and a protein-rich meal for livestock. Regional testing helped distinguish plants that could survive Great Plains winters from promising varieties adapted elsewhere. The 1995 advanced trials included lines first selected at Hays, Colby and Columbia.
crops.context: In 1997, seven sites had at least one line above 3,000 lb of seed per acre. Hays itself was not harvested because of bird damage. Those results show regional potential, rather than a Hays yield or a measured adoption benefit.

crops.name: Sorghum
crops.work: Sorghum provided a dryland benchmark for Bill’s millet work. At Hays, he also coauthored a study prompted by virus-like symptoms in sorghum and pearl millet in 1994.

parts.name: Branched grain head
parts.text: The grains sit on branches of a panicle. This drawing shows a compact grain type; panicle shape varies among sorghums.

parts.name: Grass blades
parts.text: Long grass blades spread from the upright stem. The leaf bases sheath the stem.

parts.name: Stem and nodes
parts.text: A sturdy jointed stem supports the grain head. Its nodes mark the points where leaves attach.

metrics.label: sorghum lines included in greenhouse inoculation tests
pearl millet lines in the same screening experiments

crops.impact: The team established natural infection of both crops by wheat streak mosaic virus and demonstrated transmission by wheat curl mites. Sorghum responses differed among virus isolates, showing why a single test strain could miss susceptibility.
crops.context: The study expanded the known host range and supported better disease screening. Its line counts describe experiments; the paper does not quantify farm income or crop losses prevented.
